{{Short description|Mathematical term}}
In [[nonstandard analysis]], a discipline within classical mathematics, '''microcontinuity''' (or ''S''-continuity) of an [[internal function]] ''f'' at a point ''a'' is defined as follows:
:for all ''x'' infinitely close to ''a'', the value ''f''(''x'') is infinitely close to ''f''(''a'').
Here ''x'' runs through the domain of ''f''.  In formulas, this can be expressed as follows:
:if <math>x\approx a</math> then <math>f(x)\approx f(a)</math>.

For a function ''f'' defined on <math>\mathbb{R}</math>, the definition can be expressed in terms of the [[Halo (mathematics)|halo]] as follows: ''f'' is microcontinuous at <math>c\in\mathbb{R}</math> if and only if <math>f(hal(c))\subseteq hal(f(c))</math>, where the natural extension of ''f'' to the [[hyperreal number|hyperreals]] is still denoted ''f''.  Alternatively, the property of microcontinuity at ''c'' can be expressed by stating that the composition <math>\text{st}\circ f</math> is constant on the halo of ''c'', where "st" is the [[standard part function]].

==History==

The modern property of continuity of a function was first defined by Bolzano in 1817.  However, Bolzano's work was not noticed by the larger mathematical community until its rediscovery in Heine in the 1860s.  Meanwhile, [[Cauchy]]'s textbook [[Cours d'Analyse]] defined continuity in 1821 using [[infinitesimal]]s as above.<ref>{{citation

==Continuity and uniform continuity==

The property of microcontinuity is typically applied to the natural extension ''f*'' of a real function ''f''.  Thus, ''f'' defined on a real interval ''I'' is [[Continuous function|continuous]] if and only if ''f*''  is microcontinuous at every point of ''I''.  Meanwhile, ''f'' is [[uniformly continuous]] on ''I'' if and only if ''f*'' is microcontinuous at every point (standard and nonstandard) of the natural extension ''I*'' of its domain ''I'' (see Davis, 1977, p.&nbsp;96).

==Example 1==
The real function <math>f(x)=\tfrac{1}{x}</math> on the open interval (0,1) is not uniformly continuous because the natural extension ''f*'' of ''f'' fails to be microcontinuous at an [[infinitesimal]] <math>a>0</math>.  Indeed, for such an ''a'', the values ''a'' and ''2a'' are infinitely close, but the values of ''f*'', namely <math>\tfrac{1}{a}</math> and <math>\tfrac{1}{2a}</math> are not infinitely close.

==Example 2==
The function <math>f(x)=x^2</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}</math> is not uniformly continuous because ''f*'' fails to be microcontinuous at an infinite point <math>H\in \mathbb{R}^*</math>.  Namely, setting <math>e=\tfrac{1}{H}</math> and ''K''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''H''&nbsp;+&nbsp;''e'', one easily sees that ''H'' and ''K'' are infinitely close but ''f''*(''H'') and ''f''*(''K'') are not infinitely close.

==Uniform convergence==
[[Uniform convergence]] similarly admits a simplified definition in a hyperreal setting.  Thus, a sequence <math>f_n</math> converges to ''f'' uniformly if for all ''x'' in the domain of ''f*'' and all infinite ''n'', <math>f_n^*(x)</math> is infinitely close to <math>f^*(x)</math>.
